bibliographic.title: Uncanny Semantics: How AI and Human Authors Use Language Differently in Academic Writing
bibliographic.citation_apa: Wegerhoff, D. (2026). Uncanny Semantics: How AI and Human Authors Use Language Differently in Academic Writing. AI-Linguistica, 5(1). https://doi.org/10.62408/ai-ling.v5i1.32

methodology.method_family: corpus linguistics; computational semantics; word embedding analysis
methodology.study_design: comparative corpus study of human-authored versus LLM-generated academic introductions
methodology.sample_description: 325 introductions from linguistic articles, including human-authored texts and AI-generated texts from six language models prompted in plain and academic modes
methodology.technology_context: OpenAI ChatGPT-4o and ChatGPT-4o1, Google Gemini Flash 2.0 and Gemini Flash 2.0 Thinking, DeepSeek V3 and DeepSeek V3-R1; NLTK; spaCy with de_core_news_lg; cosine similarity on lemmas

eligibility.decision_rationale: The study provides empirical evidence on semantic and epistemic differences between human and LLM-authored academic texts, but the provided text contains no focus on conversational systems, governance, accountability, audit, compliance, human oversight, or regulated high-stakes deployment contexts required for central inclusion.

appraisal.notes: Method is clearly described for a comparative corpus analysis using word embeddings and cosine similarity across six named LLMs and human texts. Ethics, limitations, and peer-review status are not evident in the excerpt provided.

cerqual.explanation: Within its own scope, methods and findings appear coherent and adequately supported by a 325-text corpus, but relevance to conversational governance in regulated LLM systems is very low; only foundational contextual value is supported by the provided text.

coding.theme: Linguistic and epistemic differences between human and LLM-generated academic writing
coding.subtheme: Pseudo-commitment and reduced epistemic modulation in LLM academic prose
rq_alignment: weak alignment: informs LLM text behavior but not conversational governance, oversight, or regulated-domain controls

synthesis.main_claim: AI-generated academic texts, especially under academic prompts, overuse positive-evaluative and methodological vocabulary and show weaker epistemic caution than human authors, a pattern described as pseudo-commitment that may explain perceived weirdness in AI academic writing.
synthesis.contribution: Empirical semantic comparison of human and six LLM outputs in a 325-introduction corpus using word embeddings and cosine similarity to characterize epistemic stance differences.
synthesis.limitations: Scope is limited to linguistic article introductions; regulated-domain, governance, and conversational-system implications are not addressed in the provided text; limitations section not visible in excerpt.
synthesis.use_in_review: Foundational contextual evidence on how LLMs produce academically styled but epistemically shallow prose; not central evidence for conversational governance, compliance, or regulated deployment.
